summary: The chair opened the double symposium by explaining that the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) is a publishing model for sharing richer biodiversity data than Darwin Core Archives allow. It mostly uses Darwin Core terms, plus some terms governed outside TDWG. Both formats share a guide, EML dataset metadata and CSV/TSV data files, but DwC-DP is not limited to cores, extensions and the star schema. title: From Observations to Interactions: iNaturalist and the Expanding Landscape of Biodiversity Data Sharing with DwC-DP

programme.title: From Observations to Interactions: iNaturalist and the Expanding Landscape of Biodiversity Data Sharing with DwC-DP
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 1)
programme.abstract: iNaturalist now hosts over 250 million biodiversity occurrence records representing more than 500,000 unique taxa—making it one of the largest platforms for community-contributed biodiversity data. Since 2012, iNaturalist has used the Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) format to share its research-grade observations with GBIF and other partners. While effective for basic occurrence sharing, DwC-A has not supported richer connections—especially organism interactions—found in the platform’s underlying data.The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) offers a new opportunity. This flexible and extensible format allows iNaturalist to represent not just Occurrences and their associated Media (images, sounds), but also relationships between those Occurrences—OrganismInteractions—such as predation, pollination, parasitism, and other vital ecological connections. This illustration uses community-generated Observation Fields that capture interactions even though these are not currently controlled fields in the core iNaturalist data model.This presentation will highlight how iNaturalist’s data maps to DwC-DP, illustrating both continuity and advancement over DwC-A. While Occurrence remains a foundational element, DwC-DP brings structure to a richer ecosystem of data, enabling iNaturalist to capture and communicate ecological knowledge that was previously invisible in shared datasets.Attendees will see a concrete comparison between the two Darwin Core formats through the lens of iNaturalist’s experience, showing how the transition enhances what can be shared without disrupting what already works. This case sets the stage for subsequent talks by establishing core concepts—Occurrences and Media—while introducing Interactions as an example of what DwC-DP newly enables. It demonstrates how the new standard supports both incremental improvements and novel capabilities for data providers and consumers alike.

title: From Flat to Structured: Enhancing Natural History Collection Datasets in GBIF Using Darwin Core Data Packages

programme.title: From Flat to Structured: Enhancing Natural History Collection Datasets in GBIF Using Darwin Core Data Packages
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 1)
programme.abstract: With a collection of currently about 4 million specimens, the Botanic Garden & Botanical Museum Berlin (BGBM) houses the largest herbarium in Germany. Complementary to this main collection, the seed bank, the DNA bank and the living collection in the botanical garden with more than 32,000 documented accessions are important components of the institution (BGBM Press 2022). The herbarium is partly digitized with high-resolution voucher images, sporadically accompanied by photographs of the respective living organism. Herbarium specimens and their images are published to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), digital records of tissues and DNA samples to the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN, Dröge et al. 2016), and extracted sequences to the International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration (INSDC, Karsch-Mizrachi et al. 2025).Until recently, GBIF was centered around the concept of occurrences using Darwin Core (Wieczorek et al. 2012) or ABCD (Access to Biological Collections Data, Holetschek et al. 2012). Although it was possible to publish material samples, their relation to the original specimen was lost. In order to overcome this limitation and to be able to model complex relationships between entities, GBIF has introduced Darwin Core Data Packages. They are based on Frictionless Data, a toolkit for transparent FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable; Wilkinson et al. 2016) data sharing. Darwin Core Data Packages will enable publishing structured biodiversity data about organisms, observations, specimens, material samples, media objects, sequences, biotic interactions – and, above all, all their complex relationships.We will discuss the results of a pilot study in which the diverse collection data of the BGBM were published to GBIF with this new approach. Darwin Core Data Packages allowed to include tissue and DNA samples and their lineage from specimens, the images of organisms before being collected, and DNA sequences – information previously not shared with GBIF.

Previously only specimens and specimen images went to GBIF, while tissue and DNA samples went to GGBN and sequences to ENA/NCBI. title: Modeling Complex Marine Survey Data Using the Darwin Core Data Package

programme.title: Modeling Complex Marine Survey Data Using the Darwin Core Data Package

speakers.name: Yi-Ming Gan
speakers.affiliation: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 1)
programme.abstract: The BROKE-West fish dataset originates from a pelagic survey conducted in the Southern Ocean during the 2006 BROKE-West voyage. Since its initial publication in 2008 as a flat Darwin Core Archive (DwCA) occurrence table, the dataset has undergone significant evolution. Although rich in associated data, the original version included only species occurrence records. In 2016, it was used to test the extended MeasurementOrFact (eMoF) extension developed by OBIS, which enabled the inclusion of environmental and biological measurements. In 2023, survey design and sampling context were incorporated through the Humboldt Extension. Today, the dataset has been fully restructured using the proposed Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP), a model that overcomes the structural limitations of the DwCA star schema. DwC-DP enables the expression of previously unpublished ancillary information and allows for the clear linkage of survey design, sampling events, occurrences, materials, community-level measurements, individual measurements, environmental measurements, and material relationships (e.g., prey items derived from stomach samples). This transformation offers a test case for evaluating how DwC-DP addresses long-standing challenges in representing complex biodiversity survey data.From the perspective of a GBIF and OBIS node, adopting this new model presents significant opportunities. DwC-DP offers a richer structure that represents the complexity of biodiversity data. However, these benefits come with challenges. DwC-DP is more complex to implement and contains more identifiers, requiring more effort in transforming and maintaining the data. This may require shifts in data modeling, tooling, and workflows. Addressing these issues through capacity building, guidance, and tooling will be important to realise DwC-DP’s full potential.

summary: Yi-Ming Gan restructured the BROKE-West fish dataset (a 2006 Southern Ocean pelagic survey, published in 2008 as a single table) as a Darwin Core Data Package of 23 tables. The model covers routine and target midwater trawl events, survey targets with taxon, life stage and body size, event assertions for net and trawl measurements, and occurrences linked to survey targets. It also covers identifications, individually preserved and photographed fish as materials with weight, length and energy-content assertions, and stomach-content prey items as derived materials with degree-of-digestion assertions. A thought experiment showed most of this could be forced into a DwC-A with Humboldt, eMoF and other extensions, but with losses: less freedom in survey targets, awkward occurrence IDs for individual fish, and media without licence metadata. The talk then demonstrated using the data: inferring non-detections from survey targets, plotting a fish-length frequency distribution (an Essential Ocean Variables sub-variable), and deriving the diet composition of Antarctic silverfish.
one_line_takeaway: DwC-DP can represent a complex legacy marine survey closer to reality and makes new derived products possible, but splitting tables and maintaining many identifiers is hard without tooling.
why_it_matters: It is a demanding stress-test of DwC-DP from a GBIF/OBIS node, showing both what is gained (survey design, materials, prey relationships, derived analyses) and the operational burden that tools must address.

A DwC-A version could hold most content via event core, Humboldt, occurrence and eMoF extensions, but with losses in survey-target expressiveness, identifier semantics and media metadata.

summary: Cecilie Svenningsen presented the mapping of Insektmobilen, a Danish national citizen-science and DNA metabarcoding survey of flying insects, from a Darwin Core Archive to a Darwin Core Data Package. In the archive, the single-core, one-layer star schema forced sampling-event data into an occurrence core so that the DNA-derived data extension could be used. As a result, media, event information, eMoF and DNA data were repeated for every occurrence; for example, a beetle occurrence showed images of the whole bulk sample. In DwC-DP, citizen scientists are agents conducting surveys with land-cover and taxon targets. Bulk samples are materials with biomass and DNA-concentration assertions, nucleotide analyses use three primer pairs, and occurrences are inferred from both morphological and DNA-based identifications. The data went from one core with four extensions to 12 DwC-DP tables.
one_line_takeaway: DwC-DP lets a metabarcoding survey link media, DNA analyses and identifications to the right events and materials instead of copying them onto every occurrence.
why_it_matters: Metabarcoding surveys are a fast-growing data type that fits the star schema badly; this case shows a concrete DwC-DP structure for them and the tools that helped build it.

In DwC-DP: agents conduct surveys with land-cover and taxon targets, follow protocols, and carry out sampling events that collect bulk insect material.
Dry-weight biomass of size fractions and DNA concentration are material assertions; nucleotide analysis used three primer pairs, with sequences from one pair matched against a reference database.
Identifications are based on both morphology and DNA sequences; the preferred identification is flagged with the isAcceptedIdentification term.

The quick reference guide and relationship explorer helped decide the order in which to prepare tables to obtain linking identifiers.

programme.abstract: Paleontological specimens can vary widely from the smallest single cell protist or pollen grain, to trays of molluscs or fossil samples from cores, slabs like preserved tree canopies or trackways, and, of course, to the largest dinosaurs. Each of these examples has inherent characteristics requiring careful consideration of how to best represent that specimen in a digital record affecting discoverability and fitness-for-use of the data. Previous work (Little 2018, Little et al. 2021) has shown that there are known challenges in mapping paleontological specimen data to existing data standards. While most biological and paleontological specimens share similar fundamental data (evidence of a taxon at a place and time collected by a person), the addition of geological context adds multidimensional complexity, and variations in the preservation of paleontological materials can impact data requirements for documenting what is present. Assessing the nuances of the data across heterogeneous paleontological specimens will help to make comprehensive recommendations for communicating their inherent complexity.Through coordination with the paleontology collections community, we are conducting an assessment to characterize the various types of paleontological specimens in our collections to document the data requirements for clearly describing them and their associated information. Our aim is to ensure consistency and discoverability in what is represented in the data and to enable better alignment with existing or developing global data practices. This effort will result in a resource consisting of example records, use cases for testing new data formats, highlights of key data classes, and implementation guidelines for standards like Darwin Core. Importantly, these results can be used to evaluate new developments like the Darwin Core Data Package to ensure paleontological specimen data can be mobilized, discovered, and used interoperably. Here we share an overview of this process and initial results.Little 2018, https:||doi.org|10.3897|biss.2.25437Little et al. 2021, https:||doi.org|10.3897|biss.5.75646

programme.abstract: After nearly two decades of success with Darwin Core and the Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A), the biodiversity informatics community faces the need to share data that are both richer in detail and deeper in structure than existing formats support. The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) emerges as a direct response to this need—not as a replacement, but as a natural, practical evolution of a trusted standard. This presentation introduces DwC-DP as the result of six years of iterative, use case–driven development and testing, designed to extend the capabilities of Darwin Core without discarding its simplicity or adoption base.The journey began with the Unified Model—a comprehensive conceptual design proven to meet complex use cases, but too burdensome for everyday use. DwC-DP captures the “sweet spot” of that design: flexible enough to support emerging data types (e.g., Nucleotide Analyses, Organism Interactions, Survey Targets, Phylogenetic Trees), while retaining usability for current data publishers.Key features include modular schemas, a clearly event-based structure, and reusable extension patterns for concepts like Agent Roles, Media, Assertions, Protocols, and References. DwC-DP supports both flattened and nested forms, empowering users to adopt the level of complexity appropriate to their data.This talk will demystify DwC-DP for audiences ranging from cautious data providers to advanced integrators, highlighting its role as a community-informed technical foundation—supported by GBIF, governed by TDWG, and shaped by global feedback. Attendees will leave with a clearer sense of how DwC-DP enables more science and better decision-making without requiring a disruptive shift for those already using Darwin Core.

programme.abstract: ABCD (Access to Biological Collection Data, https:||abcd.tdwg.org|) is a TDWG (Biodiversity Information Standards) standard that was developed by a broad international collaboration to create a structured framework for capturing and exchanging biodiversity data.ABCD was implemented as a hierarchical XML schema, allowing it to interoperate seamlessly with standardized software components. This design enables diverse applications such as data publication, harvesting and aggregation, quality control, and access through data portals. By facilitating harmonized exchange and integration of primary biodiversity data, ABCD supports robust scientific workflows and analyses (Holetschek et al. 2012, https:||doi.org|10.1080|11263504.2012.740085).Over the past two decades, ABCD has undergone continuous refinement to align with the evolving needs of the biodiversity informatics community. In parallel with the widely used Darwin Core standard (Wieczorek et al. 2012, https:||doi.org|10.1371|journal.pone.0029715), ABCD plays a vital role in promoting the harmonization, mobilization, and dissemination of biodiversity data across both national and international infrastructures. Domain-specific extensions for ABCD play a central role for special-interest networks, like the Global Genome Biodiversity Network (GGBN, Droege et al. 2016, https:||doi.org|10.1093|database|baw125). An important example of the use of ABCD at the national level is the establishment of standardized data flows between domain data centers and central aggregation and data analysis platforms in NFDI4Biodiversity in Germany (Glöckner et al. 2020, https:||doi.org|10.5281|zenodo.3943645).The latest iteration of the standard, ABCD version 3.0, introduces a significant architectural enhancement: the semantic definitions of data elements are now decoupled from their structural representation in XML. This modularization promotes greater flexibility in how the standard can be applied and reused, facilitating integration into emerging data ecosystems and enhancing interoperability (Fichtmueller et al. 2019, https:||doi.org|10.3897|biss.3.37214). In particular, ABCD contributes to the emerging "Darwin Core Data Package" a new initiative aimed at enabling the global exchange and reuse of structured collection and observational data based on Frictionless Data technology (https:||frictionlessdata.io|).

summary: Anton Güntsch traced the history of biodiversity data models. About 30 years ago, comprehensive relational reference models (e.g. Walter Berendsohn's model for collections and surveys) were used mainly for local databases, while early networks such as the Species Analyst (Z39.50) and the European natural history specimen information network used much simpler models. XML was then agreed as the right balance of comprehensibility and expressiveness. That led to ABCD, developed between 2001 and 2006: comprehensive, highly hierarchical, with extension slots for networks such as GGBN, and now about 100 provider installations, more than 10 special-interest networks, integration into GBIF, and use in NFDI4Biodiversity. ABCD 3.0 made it a semantic standard. Güntsch argued that DwC-DP's relational structure realises the original relational vision. The ABCD/BioCASe community will help develop and maintain DwC-DP, build templates, and extend the BioCASe help desk to complex DwC-DP data.
one_line_takeaway: For the ABCD/BioCASe community, DwC-DP fulfils the long-held aim of exchanging relational biodiversity data, and they will actively support it.
why_it_matters: It places DwC-DP in a 30-year lineage of biodiversity data models and commits a major existing standard community and its help desk to supporting the transition rather than competing with it.

title: Seamless Integration: How DiSSCo's openDS Facilitates Data Interoperability with the Darwin Core Data Package

programme.title: Seamless Integration: How DiSSCo's openDS Facilitates Data Interoperability with the Darwin Core Data Package
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The Distributed System for Scientific Collection (DiSSCo) has been following the developments of the Darwin Core Conceptual Model and the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) with great interest. DiSSCo is an emerging European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC) aimed at accelerating the digitisation of Europe's Natural History Collections. Vital to this acceleration is the exchange of knowledge, ideas, and tools, which can be done through the DiSSCo infrastructure. Essential for the infrastructure is a collective language in the form of data standards, which we call open Digital Specimen (openDS).The development of openDS has been done in parallel to the development of the Darwin Core Conceptual Model. OpenDS has reached production maturity after it has gone through a public review in 2024. OpenDS is a document focussed specification optimized for data curation, where each document represents a Fair Digital Object (FDO). This means that openDS is broader than the specimen information but also contains models to capture annotations and provenance. As the openDS Digital Specimen and Digital Media models are developed on top of existing TDWG standards and the work on the Darwin Core Conceptual Model, they can be seen as an implementation of the conceptual model. Translations between openDS and DwC-DP, both implementations of the conceptual model, can therefore be made without any loss in data.During the session, DiSSCo will share their experience with implementing both the conceptual model in the form of openDS and the translation from openDS to the DwC-DP. DiSSCo will be able to create DwC-DP for any of their data, showing how specimen from Natural History Collections can be mapped to DwC-DP.

summary: Sam Leeflang explained that DiSSCo aims to create FAIR Digital Objects as digital extended specimens. In 2022, rather than invent yet another standard, DiSSCo chose to align its open Digital Specimen (openDS) specification with the GBIF Unified Model, and later with the Darwin Core conceptual model. openDS went through public review and is now in production. It is described as a separate, specimen-specific implementation of the conceptual model: document-oriented, denormalised JSON optimised for mutating single specimens. DwC-DP, in contrast, is a full, normalised tabular reference implementation. DiSSCo mapped almost all openDS terms to about 23 DwC-DP schemas, and any dataset in its acceptance environment can now be downloaded as a DwC-A or DwC-DP (the largest about 750,000 records). Identifiers implicit in nested documents had to be created with MD5 hashes and temporary tables.
one_line_takeaway: Because openDS was built on the same conceptual model, DiSSCo can transform specimen data to DwC-DP with almost no loss, needing only generated identifiers.
why_it_matters: It shows that two different serialisations of the Darwin Core conceptual model — document-oriented for curation and tabular for transport — can interoperate nearly losslessly, supporting the case that the conceptual model works as a common language.

title: Implementation Status of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC DP) at GBIF

programme.title: Implementation Status of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC DP) at GBIF
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The implementation of the Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) goes beyond enabling publishing mechanisms,i t also benefits from data services that support search, discovery, and exploration. GBIF.org currently offers a robust data indexing platform, including an API and data portal. A large proportion of the available data has been published using the existing Darwin Core Archive (DwC-A) standard. While DwC-A’s simplicity has enabled effective aggregation within a centralized infrastructure, the richer modeling capabilities of the new DwC-DP introduce both opportunities and challenges for future data services.To address this, the GBIF Secretariat is developing a phased roadmap for data ingestion and discovery services based on the new DwC-DP. The roadmap includes: enabling the publishing and registration of DwC-DP datasets; extending dataset catalogs to support discovery; facilitating exploration of dataset structures and schemas; and, in the near future, implementing global data services for cross-dataset querying and downloads, comparable to those currently available on GBIF.org.This presentation provides a status update on the development of this roadmap. It demonstrates how a DwC-DP dataset can be published, ingested, and explored through its internal structure via a test data portal. Finally, it outlines upcoming service enhancements for both the current DwC-A platform and the evolving DwC-DP based infrastructure.

title: Implementing the proposed DwC-DP format in GBIF: data publishing tools

programme.title: Implementing the proposed DwC-DP format in GBIF: data publishing tools
programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The GBIF Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT) has enabled the publication of thousands of datasets in a robust and user-friendly way for more than a decade. This success is due in part to the simplicity and clarity of the Darwin Core standard, as well as the straightforward workflows the IPT provides for data publishers.As the data model supporting the mobilization of more complex biodiversity data evolves, so too must the infrastructure. Traditional schemas like Darwin Core have served the community well, but they limit the expression of richer biodiversity information. To address this, GBIF is working towards introducing the new Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP), designed to better represent complex relationships among biodiversity entities. While DwC-DP opens exciting possibilities for linking entities and supporting diverse data types, it also presents significant challenges for developers and data publishers. We must balance this increased richness with usability, ensuring that tools like the IPT remain accessible to a broad community. Key challenges include managing data model versions, providing user guidance for complex schemas, and ensuring that schema governance and validation workflows are transparent and sustainable.This presentation will offer a vision for implementing DwC-DP support in the IPT, including design decisions, current state and limitations, and planned improvements.We aim to inspire contributions and ideas from the TDWG community to improve tooling and practices, ultimately helping to lower the barriers to publishing high-quality, richly structured biodiversity datasets.

summary: Mikhail Podolskiy, lead developer of GBIF's Integrated Publishing Toolkit (IPT), discussed the user-interface challenges of supporting DwC-DP: a large, overwhelming new model, many identifiers and join tables, and identifier maintenance. title: Darwin Core Data Package public review process

programme.session: Darwin Core Data Package: an updated model and format for exchanging biodiversity data (Part 2)
programme.abstract: The TDWG Vocabulary Maintenance Specification (VMS, http:||rs.tdwg.org|vms|doc|specification|) provides a mechanism for making a set of coordinated changes to a vocabulary. The Darwin Core Data Package (DwC-DP) falls into this category of coordinated additions to the Darwin Core standard (http:||www.tdwg.org|standards|450). In this presentation, I will describe how the public review process described by the VMS applies to the DwC-DP proposal. Specifically, I will detail: what is under review, how the proposed changes will be added to the standard and its documentation, and how the public can provide comments to participate in the public review.

summary: Steve Baskauf, convenor of the Darwin Core Maintenance Group, explained how the DwC-DP proposal is being reviewed under the TDWG Vocabulary Maintenance Specification. Anyone may propose changes; the maintenance group assesses demand, efficacy and stability, then opens a public comment period seeking consensus, and the Executive Committee ratifies. Because DwC-DP is a vocabulary enhancement beyond the basic term layer, it required user feedback documents. Under review are two documents, the conceptual model and the data package guide (based on Frictionless Data Packages), plus related term additions and changes. Implementation details such as how data packages are actually built are outside the standard. The review opened in September and runs at least until 16 December: 90 days instead of the usual 30 because of the proposal's complexity. Comments go to GitHub issues, reached via a landing page and per-class issue summaries, or by email to the convenor.
one_line_takeaway: The DwC-DP proposal is in an extended 90-day TDWG public review covering the conceptual model, the data package guide and related term changes, with comments taken on GitHub or by email.

summary: The closing discussion began with whether the public review receives adequate comments. The panel feared the community is not yet educated enough to comment meaningfully on such a complex, interdependent proposal, where a lack of consensus on one part could cascade. Issue summaries let people focus on what matters to them, Erica Krimmel had volunteered to host 'Darwin Core hours', and GitHub thumbs-up reactions are a useful way to signal agreement. A suggestion that thematic communities propose and endorse IPT dataset profiles led Tim Robertson to recount how community-specific publishing models (ColDP, Camtrap DP) were dropped after fragmentation concerns, only for profiles to re-emerge as the unified model felt overwhelming. Tim also said metabarcoding DwC-As reach half a terabyte because of star-schema repetition, and DwC-DP can shrink them about a thousandfold. Other questions covered nested trait assertions (not supported; would need a new term), a forum for unusual use cases, project-level metadata (no project class yet), and building expertise through training and the TDWG review.
one_line_takeaway: Panellists acknowledged that review participation, model complexity and expertise are real constraints, while arguing that metabarcoding scale makes something like DwC-DP operationally necessary.
why_it_matters: The discussion reveals open design gaps (recursive assertions, project class), governance risks in the review, and the operational driver (metabarcoding data volume) behind GBIF's implementation priorities.
key_points: Review participation: fair so far but uneven; the community may not be educated enough to comment meaningfully; no consensus means a proposal is excluded, and interdependencies could cascade.
Issue summaries were a new way of organising issues so that interested people can go directly to the parts that matter to them.
Erica Krimmel had volunteered to host 'Darwin Core hours' for education and discussion (not yet scheduled).
GitHub thumbs-up reactions are the built-in way to signal agreement without flooding issues with comments.
Steve Baskauf replied in the chat (relayed by the chair) that the number of comments depends on the topic.
Dataset profiles: GBIF would implement the concept and communities would decide on and manage their own profiles; the user guide aims to give domain-specific starting points.

Tim Robertson: community-specific publishing models (ColDP for checklists, Camtrap DP) were discouraged as fragmenting; a single model became overwhelming; simplified profiles may return, integrable through the conceptual model.
Metabarcoding DwC-As with about 27 million detections reach half a terabyte due to star-schema repetition; the same data as DwC-DP via the MDT can be about a thousand times smaller.
GBIF may need to implement part of DwC-DP specifically to support metabarcoding even if not everything at once.
No recursive relationship on assertions yet for nested trait measurements; a workaround exists but a related-assertion identifier term could be added given a strong use case.
Model experts have been helping with unusual use cases for over a year and will continue; the goal is to produce more experts.
No project class yet; project information is limited to EML or project names/IDs in provenance; a project class could be developed.
Building expertise: an internal GBIF node-manager training (correcting the Part 1 workshop answer), bringing the work to TDWG, keeping the community together; training materials are freely available.

q_and_a.question: Nikki asked what coverage of people submit comments in review periods and whether commenting is adequate.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): a big worry for this complex proposal; simpler reviews get plenty of interaction, but complex topics can fail to reach consensus, and interdependencies could cascade; the community may not be educated enough; issue summaries help people focus; participation so far is fair. Another speaker noted Erica Krimmel volunteered to host Darwin Core hours. Later the chair relayed Steve Baskauf's chat reply that comment numbers depend on the topic.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether there is a way to state agreement with the model or parts of it during the review.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed: use the thumbs-up reactions on issues; it is useful feedback and helps show what matters to people.

q_and_a.question: An audience member suggested to Mikhail ('Misha') that thematic communities could be called on to propose and endorse IPT dataset profiles.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Mikhail Podolskiy: GBIF would implement the profile concept and communities would decide and manage their own profiles. An unidentified speaker added that the user guide aims to provide domain-specific starting points. Tim Robertson described the history of community-specific models (ColDP, Camtrap DP), fragmentation concerns, the return of simplified profiles, and the metabarcoding size problem.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked how DwC-DP accommodates nested trait measurements (e.g. leaves grouped by branch within a specimen).
q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): no recursive relationship on assertions; it was considered but lacked a strong use case; a workaround is possible but unclear; adding a related-assertion ID term would be simple — bring a good use case.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether there is a forum where people with unusual use cases can talk through mappings with experts on the proposed model.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): this has been done for over a year and will continue; the hope is to produce more experts, and the answerer will be available to help for at least the next year.

q_and_a.question: Lynn asked where project-level metadata should be mapped in DwC-DP — EML or the highest-level events.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Unattributed (probably John Wieczorek): a project class was investigated but not implemented for lack of a use case; GBIF sees demand; currently only EML or project names/IDs in provenance; a project class can be developed.

q_and_a.question: Nikki asked how the team plans to develop more experts.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Tim Robertson: by sharing the work at this conference and bringing it to TDWG; GBIF held an internal training for node managers (correcting an earlier statement) to build capacity that can spread to their communities; the community must be kept together; ideas are welcome. The chair added that the training materials are freely available online.
